coherence.reasons: Both follow the same sound hierarchy: a quantified diagnosis, why the hour cut fails, lever-by-lever sizing, then a plan that adds up. X's five summary points map cleanly onto its five sections and its plan arithmetic reconciles (15.3 + 29.6 = 44.9 on $1,412M). But X's governing thought of about 3.2% by FY2028 is undercut by its own evidence: the 2027 wage rise it names as the main risk would leave margin near 2.7%, below target, with no answer. X also says six stores close at expiry yet counts all nine exits in the headline, and says the covenant is 'cleared' at roughly $20.1M against $20M. Y's hierarchy holds together better: base plan of six exits, confidence ratings, FY2026 phasing to about $27M, and contingency levers that close the wage gap. Y has small slips: a '≤$17.5M' one-time cost that includes the non-base three stores, a promotion cut rated Medium but listed among high-confidence levers, and one slide whose title is a label rather than a claim.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the management draft and land on the answer key's preferred recommendation (R1) with targeted labor. Y weighs the trade-offs better. It cuts promotions only to 26% and keeps events in ValuMart trade areas with a monthly comp trigger to restore them, whereas X goes all the way back to 24% on the assumption that de-promoted sales stay at regular price. Y separates the six lease-end exits from the three that need a vote and $7.5M, computes the roughly 3.4-year payback and holds them as contingency; X puts all nine in the base plan without testing that trade-off. Y phases FY2026 to about $27M with about $7M of covenant headroom, while X's 'quarter of run-rate' gives essentially none. Y sizes contingency levers of $7.6M against the wage rise; X simply reports that the plan would fall to 2.7%. Y also rates lever confidence, shows the downside if only high-confidence levers deliver (about 2.0%), budgets one-time cost and frames explicit board decisions. X's alternatives section is thinner and leaves the $25M cap uncosted.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core calculations right: the margin bridge with labor at 13%, the e-commerce loss of $10.4M reconciled to the $18.1M fulfillment line, the fee test roll-out, the $6.6M store-exit gain, and the debunking of the 6.1% claim. X's weaknesses are mostly over-confident inferences. It calls the $7.5M shrink leak 'cautious' although it rests on a time-series coincidence. It infers that 5% of sales can come from losing events alone by comparing a share of sales with a share of events. It assumes all de-promoted sales stay at regular price. Its $6.8M store-hours figure (shrink $3.5M + hours $3.6M − $0.4M) is opaque, and one-time costs are unestimated. Y is more careful: it labels the $10M shrink leak an upper bound because theft is 35% of shrink, calls the category team's claim correlation, nets the provider's 3% rate rise out of the fee gain, and discloses the pro-rata store split and its assumptions. Y's own weak points are the vendor-funding lever, which rests on an interpretive assumption about the 14-point gap, and the targeted-labor $5.2M, which is 3% of the whole labor bill but described as a cut in high-labor stores. It also uses the pack's price-perception and private-label trend evidence more fully.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CFO/COO hypothesis as the answer key expects. Each shows wages rose 9.4% while hours per $1,000 fell 6%, so labor explains only 13% of the fall, and each uses the shrink-by-quartile table to argue against the across-the-board cut while keeping a targeted trim in the best-staffed stores. X gives the labor argument a dedicated slide and credits what management got right about wage rates. Y goes a little further on both halves of the draft. It links the past hours reduction to the shrink rise with an explicit caveat. It shows the draft's range of 1.3–2.0% and its covenant exposure. And it replaces the e-commerce freeze with a rule that volume grows only where each order covers its cost, then asks the board to withdraw the cut formally. X also rejects the freeze but only through repricing. The difference is small.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, correctly diagnosed, sized plans that reach about 3.2%. Y would serve the CEO better in front of the board and the lender. Its base plan is more conservative and needs no board vote on the long-lease stores. It shows FY2026 phasing with real covenant headroom, estimates one-time cost against the $25M cap, and rates confidence by lever. It also has sized contingencies that keep the plan above 3.0% after the 2027 wage rise, which is exactly where X's plan falls to 2.7% with no answer. X is tighter and its arithmetic is clean, but it relies on a full return to 24% promotions despite ValuMart, assumes all nine exits, and clears the covenant only on paper.
